The elder and his churches
Where the letters were read, who 3 John names, and the questions readers still ask.
ON THE MAP
Ephesus and the churches of Asia
Ephesus and the churches of Asia, by tradition.

None of the three letters names a place. Early tradition sets John at Ephesus late in his life, and the letters are usually linked with the churches of the province of Asia around it.[15][16][11][24][3][2]

IN TIME
The three heavenly witnesses
How the "three that bear record in heaven" entered the printed Bible.

The King James Version, following the printed Greek text of its day, includes these words. Nearly all Greek manuscripts and the oldest translations do not have them, and 19th-century textual critics such as Westcott, Scrivener, Plummer and Brooke concluded they entered from a Latin note. A minority of earlier writers, such as John Gill, defended them. Dates are as these critics report them. 1 John 5:7–8 [1][7][3][2][8]
OPEN QUESTIONS
Where readers have differed
5 questions about these letters. Each answer is shown with the people who held it; this page does not choose between them.
The apostle John wrote all three
Irenaeus (c. 180); Dionysius of Alexandria for 1 John (c. 250s); B. F. Westcott; A. Plummer; Robert Law; William Smith; M. G. Easton

Irenaeus quotes 1 and 2 John as the work of “John, the disciple of the Lord”. Westcott argues that “the elder” marks a unique standing and fits the aged apostle, and Law notes that an apostle could call himself an elder, as Peter does. Plummer holds that the case for 2 John carries 3 John with it. 1 Peter 5:1 2 John 1:1 3 John 1:1 [18][13][1][3][5][10][9]
The apostle wrote 1 John; John the Elder wrote 2 and 3 John
“Many” in Jerome's day (392); raised as an open question by Eusebius (c. 325); A. E. Brooke (1912)

Papias, as quoted by Eusebius, names two Johns: the apostle, and “the presbyter John”, a disciple of the Lord. Eusebius adds the report of two tombs at Ephesus, each called John's. Jerome says many held the last two letters to be the presbyter's. Brooke finds this best supported by tradition and by the letters themselves, while leaving the Elder's relation to the apostle an unsolved mystery. 2 John 1:1 3 John 1:1 [11][19][2]
Different hands, or none of them the apostle's
Joseph Scaliger (1540–1609); F. C. Baur, H. J. Holtzmann, Pfleiderer and von Soden, as reported by Robert Law (1915)

Scaliger rejected all three letters as not the apostle's. Baur and others argued that the Gospel and 1 John had different authors, Baur explaining the likeness as imitation; Jülicher, Wrede and Wernle, by contrast, accepted a single author.[5][2]
